posts.title: Adab Before Knowledge
posts.excerpt: Why the scholars of the past began with manners, and what that means for the first lessons we give our children.
posts.standfirst: The scholars of the past taught manners before they taught texts. That order still makes sense at the kitchen table.
posts.body:
It is famously reported that when the young Malik ibn Anas, who would become the Imam of Madinah, was ready to begin seeking knowledge, his mother dressed him in fine clothes, placed a turban on his head and told him to go to his teacher Rabi'ah and learn his adab before his knowledge.

She was not telling him that manners matter more than knowledge. She was telling him that manners are the vessel knowledge is carried in. A child who has learned to listen, to respect a teacher and to be patient will receive far more from every lesson that follows.

## What adab looks like at home

For our children, adab is not a separate subject. It is the way they greet us in the morning, the way they speak to a younger sibling, the way they sit when the Qur'an is recited. It is learned mostly by watching, and only partly by being told.

- Begin with salam. Return it fully and warmly, every time.
- Teach one manner a week, and practise it together until it becomes ordinary.
- Praise the effort quietly, and correct in private.

> يَا أَيُّهَا الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا قُوا أَنفُسَكُمْ وَأَهْلِيكُمْ نَارًا
>
> "O you who believe, protect yourselves and your families from a Fire."
>
> — Surah At-Tahrim, 66:6

## Starting small

A short, regular lesson does more than a long one that never repeats. Many parents find a book with one manner per lesson helps them stay consistent: read it together, talk about one example from your own day, and agree on how you will practise it.

Adab is slow work. It is also the work that makes every other lesson easier.

posts.title: Reading the Best of Stories with Our Children
posts.excerpt: Allah calls the story of Yusuf 'alaihis salam the best of stories. Here is how we read it with young children.
posts.standfirst: Allah Himself calls the story of Yusuf 'alaihis salam the best of stories. It is a gift to read it with our children.
posts.body:
Surah Yusuf opens with a promise. Allah tells His Messenger ﷺ that He will relate to him the best of stories. Few passages in the Qur'an follow one person's life so closely, from a child's dream to a reunion many years later.

> نَحْنُ نَقُصُّ عَلَيْكَ أَحْسَنَ الْقَصَصِ
>
> "We relate to you the best of stories."
>
> — Surah Yusuf, 12:3

## Why children connect with it

Children understand this story quickly. There are brothers who feel jealous, a father who loves deeply, a long wait and a moment of forgiveness. Each of these is part of a child's own world.

What they may not yet see is the thread of sabr and trust in Allah that runs through every scene. Yusuf is wronged again and again, yet he never stops being truthful, patient and kind.

## Reading it together

- Tell it in short parts over several evenings, so each scene has room to settle.
- Pause at the hard moments and ask, "What would you have felt?"
- End each part with one lesson in a sentence your child can repeat.

The surah ends by reminding us that in these stories is a lesson for people of understanding. Our task as parents is simply to open the door to that lesson, and let the Qur'an do its work.

posts.title: Tawakkul and the Birds
posts.excerpt: The hadith our name comes from, and what it teaches about effort and trust.
posts.standfirst: The hadith our name comes from, and why trust in Allah never means sitting still.
posts.body:
Our name comes from a hadith that many of us learned as children. The Prophet ﷺ said that if we relied on Allah as He truly deserves to be relied upon, He would provide for us as He provides for the birds.

> "They go out hungry in the morning and return full in the evening."
>
> — Jami' at-Tirmidhi, 2344

## The birds go out

It is easy to miss the most important detail. The birds do not wait in their nests. They leave in the morning, they search and they fly. Their tawakkul is not the absence of effort; it is effort made with a calm heart.

The same lesson appears in another well-known narration, where a man asked whether he should tie his camel or simply trust in Allah. He was told to tie it and trust.

## For parents

Raising children is full of effort we cannot measure and outcomes we cannot control. We choose their books, we teach, we correct, we pray. Then we leave the results with Allah.

That is the spirit we hope to bring to every book we share: do your part well, and trust Allah with the rest.

posts.title: Choosing the Right Level for Your Child
posts.excerpt: A simple guide to matching Quranic Tarbiyah levels to your child's age and reading stage.
posts.standfirst: A simple guide to matching each Quranic Tarbiyah level to your child, and what to do when age and ability don't line up.
posts.body:
One of the questions we are asked most often is which level to buy. The Quranic Tarbiyah series is organised so that each level matches one year of age, which makes a good starting point.

- Level 1: around age 5
- Level 2: around age 6
- Level 3: around age 7
- Level 4: around age 8
- Level 5: around age 9

## When age and ability differ

Children are not all the same. A confident reader may enjoy a level above their age, while a child who is new to Islamic lessons may settle better one level below. The goal is a book your child can enjoy with you, not one that feels like a test.

If you are reading aloud, you can usually go a level higher. If your child will read alone, choose the level where they can read most words without help.

## Siblings

Because the four subjects run side by side, siblings can each have their own level of the same subject. Everyone studies adab, or the Sirah, in the same week, and conversations at dinner become shared.

Still unsure? Send us a message on Instagram with your child's age and reading stage, and we will gladly help you choose.

posts.title: A Ten-Minute Family Reading Routine
posts.excerpt: Ten minutes after Maghrib, one book and a few good questions. A routine any family can keep.
posts.standfirst: Ten minutes after Maghrib, one book and a few good questions. A routine small enough to keep.
posts.body:
Most families we speak to want to read Islamic books with their children. Few have the time for long lessons. The good news is that a short routine kept every day does more than an ambitious one kept once a month.

## The routine

- **Same time, same place.** After Maghrib works well for many families: the day is winding down and everyone is home.
- **One book, one lesson.** Read a single lesson or story, and stop while your child still wants more.
- **Two questions.** Ask what happened, then ask what we can do because of it.
- **One du'a.** End by making du'a together, even a short one.

## Keep it light

Children remember how a lesson felt long after they forget its details. Sit close, let them turn the pages, and laugh when the story allows it. The aim is for them to look forward to these ten minutes.

Some evenings will be missed. That is fine. Return to it the next day without guilt, and let the habit grow at its own pace.

posts.title: Building a Small Islamic Library at Home
posts.excerpt: You don't need many books. You need the right few, within reach, and a reason to open them.
posts.standfirst: You don't need many books. You need the right few, within reach, and a reason to open them.
posts.body:
A home library does not have to be a room, or even a full shelf. For most families, a dozen well-chosen books placed where children can reach them will do more than a hundred kept out of sight.

> وَقُل رَّبِّ زِدْنِي عِلْمًا
>
> "And say: My Lord, increase me in knowledge."
>
> — Surah Ta-Ha, 20:114

## A balanced shelf

- **Stories of the prophets and the Sirah,** so children know the people they are meant to love.
- **Qur'an and tadabbur,** so recitation comes with meaning.
- **Adab and character,** so faith shows in daily life.
- **One or two books just for joy,** so reading never feels only like study.

## Making it inviting

Face a few covers outward and change them every week or two. Keep a basket by the sofa for the books you are reading now. When a child sees a book often, they will eventually ask about it.

Start with what you have, add slowly and choose well. A small library, used daily, is a beautiful thing to give a child.
